# Question Answering Skill

## Workflow

1. Read the clue and identify the answer slot: phrasing such as "this [kind]", "these [items]", or "this type of [category]" names the kind of answer expected and its grammatical shape — a plural noun for "these [items]", a bare name for "this [kind]", a numeral for "how many".
2. Resolve the clue to the single entity that satisfies every stated constraint at once (era, nationality, medium, relationship). For indirect clues, name the thing the clue describes at the specificity it asks for — not a famous related proper noun, and not the broad category it belongs to.
3. Reduce the candidate to its shortest canonical form: bare name, exact title, standard term, bare numeral. Drop any generic head noun or qualifier that only restates the clue's own wording.
4. Put only that string inside the `answer` element.

## Common Failure Shapes

- Clues that describe a group by its members ("the alliance of these [member type]") want the member type, not the organization's proper name.
- "These [items]" clues have a small intended set: give the canonical member or two, not an exhaustive list of everything that qualifies.
- A two-word answer whose second word merely echoes the clue's category ("[distinguishing term] [generic category]") is usually one word too long.
- Clues that are only a bare list of names (`[name], [name]`) or a name plus an event (`[name] for [event]`) carry no other context words: the answer is the specific detail those items share or the specific thing the event points to, not the generic office, class, or role they all obviously hold. When the listed items are rulers or historic figures, name the country, realm, or field they are associated with, not the family or dynasty they both happen to belong to.
- Clues that pair a category label with a short quoted title ("A [category]: '[title]'") may hide the answer in the title itself — check whether a word in the title is a name or term that fits the category, and do not default to the people associated with the work.
- Terse clues can encode the answer in their format rather than name it: a bare abbreviation after a colon (`[phrase]: [ABBR]`) asks for the full name the abbreviation stands for, located via the phrase, not an object the phrase evokes; a quoted fragment containing an ellipsis asks for the missing piece or the full title, not a repeat of the given words. Decode the format before answering, and do not grab the famous thing the clue's wording merely brings to mind.
- A clue that is nothing but a quoted line of verse or a famous saying, with no framing words around it, asks for the person behind it (its author or speaker) or the specific thing the line plainly names — never a work whose title merely repeats a word from the quote.

## Answer Form

- People: the form a reference work would use as the entry name, e.g. `[first name] [last name]`; keep a title or byname that is conventionally attached (`Sir [name]`, `Saint [name]`, `[name] the Great`), but never invent one the sources usually omit.
- Works: exact title, keeping any leading article that belongs to the title.
- Places, concepts, things: standard term, lowercase unless a proper noun.
- Quantities: the bare numeral.
- A few words at most, never a clause; nothing inside `answer` other than the answer.

attempts.approach: Added one Common Failure Shapes bullet stating that a clue that is nothing but a quoted catchphrase (no other context) asks for the person or character it is associated with, not a work whose title reuses those exact words.

bare-catchphrase-clue-answered-with-look.description: For a clue consisting only of a quoted catchphrase, the agent returned a work whose title reuses those exact words instead of the person/character the catchphrase identifies.
bare-catchphrase-clue-answered-with-look.evidence: Trajectory [9]: clue "Yabba Dabba Do!" answered "I Yabba-Dabba Do!" (EM=0, F1=0.000); the zero overlap with the gold shows the gold is not a title containing those words but the entity the catchphrase points to. The current terse-format bullet only enumerates abbreviation-after-colon and ellipsis fragments, so a bare quotation is uncovered.
bare-catchphrase-clue-answered-with-look.label: bare-catchphrase-clue-answered-with-lookalike-title

attempts.approach: Added Error Avoidance rule instructing that bare-list clues be answered with the narrower uniting property (initial letter, region, era) rather than the broad obvious class.

Added a Common Failure Shapes bullet covering bare-list ('name, name') and 'name for event' clues, stating that with no other context words the answer is the specific detail the items share or the specific thing the event points to, not the generic office/class/role they obviously hold.

Relocated the accepted bare-list / "name for event" bullet out of the orphaned position below Answer Form and into Common Failure Shapes, so it reads as a resolution procedure rather than an answer-form convention; wording unchanged.

Appended a realm-vs-dynasty clause to the existing bare-list "name, name" bullet: when the listed items are rulers or historic figures, answer with the country/realm/field they share, not the family or dynasty they both happen to belong to.

bare-list-obvious-superordinate.description: Agent answers a bare two-item place list with the obvious overarching country instead of the narrower specific attribute the items share that the gold names.
bare-list-obvious-superordinate.evidence: Trajectory [2]: clue "In Dijon & Bordeaux" answered "France" (EM=0, F1=0.000) — the generic shared country, not the specific detail the gold points to, despite the accepted Common Failure Shapes bare-list bullet.
bare-list-obvious-superordinate.examples_state_evidence: The corresponding skill entry is the Common Failure Shapes bullet on bare lists ("Clues that are only a bare list of names ([name], [name]) or a name plus an event ... name the country, realm, or field they are associated with, not the family or dynasty they both happen to belong to"). It is written with abstract category words and placeholder [name] slots only; there is no filled-in concrete pair such as "Spain" not "the House of Bourbon" attached to it.
bare-list-obvious-superordinate.label: bare-list-obvious-superordinate
bare-list-obvious-superordinate.resolve_evidence: Trajectory [13]: bare list "Inspector Luger,Wojo,Fish" was answered "Barney Miller" — the specific work the listed characters share — rather than the obvious superordinate class (detectives/TV characters), demonstrating correct bare-list handling.

bare-title-list-answered-with-containing.description: For a clue consisting only of three bare quoted song titles, the agent returned the musical that contains them, giving zero token overlap with the gold and leaving no clue-internal way to recover the intended referent.
bare-title-list-answered-with-containing.evidence: Trajectory [7]: clue "Make Believe","Cotton Blossom","Can't Help Lovin' Dat Man" -> "Show Boat" (EM=0, F1=0.000). Zero overlap means the gold is neither "Show Boat" nor any word in it; the clue carries no other constraint (no era, no writer, no category label), so no answer-form rule can discriminate the intended referent. If the gold differs only by word-splitting ("Showboat"), this would instead be an answer-format case, which is equally not fixable by adding a resolution rule.
bare-title-list-answered-with-containing.label: bare-title-list-answered-with-containing-work

descriptive-gloss-for-terse-clue.description: Agent answers a terse single-word clue with a descriptive definitional phrase rather than a short canonical term.
descriptive-gloss-for-terse-clue.evidence: Trajectory [9]: clue "Hamburg" answered "second-largest city in Germany" (F1=0.400); the gold form is not recoverable from the clue and the no-patch run scored this case correctly, so this may be sampling noise.
descriptive-gloss-for-terse-clue.label: descriptive-gloss-for-terse-clue

attempts.approach: Added Error Avoidance rule forbidding filler modifiers and clue echo, with instruction to keep looking for the exact subtype the clue points at.

Rewrote Workflow step 3 to drop an appended category word or qualifier the clue did not ask for, while explicitly preserving category words fixed in the name (e.g. [name] Island, [name] Park) so the correct successes in this batch are protected.

Revised Workflow step 3 to drop a trailing word/phrase that merely describes or narrows the entity (the business it is in, or the specific instance a general term applies to) while preserving category words fixed in the name, and added a Common Failure Shapes bullet stating 'the term/word for…' clues want the term itself, not the term plus the example instance.

Concretized the existing "two-word answer whose second word echoes the clue's category" bullet with a nickname trigger ("nicknamed this") plus a category word already present in the clue, instructing the agent to emit the distinctive phrase on its own; the edit is keyed narrowly so it is inert on the 13 correct trajectories in this batch.

Appended one clause to the existing two-word-echo bullet: when the clue names the category outright in quotation marks (e.g. "this comic 'network'"), give only the distinguishing term and do not repeat the quoted category word; the trigger is scoped to quoted category words so fixed name words are not over-stripped the way the earlier broad strip rules were.

filler-adjective-clue-echo.description: Agent returns a longer-than-gold form on a bare-term clue, either repeating the category word the clue itself quotes or keeping a descriptive adjective the clue did not ask for.
filler-adjective-clue-echo.evidence: Trajectory [1]: clue "...for writing for this comic \"network\"" -> "SCTV Network", where the gold is the single token "SCTV" (F1=2/3 = exactly one shared token), i.e. the agent repeated the clue's own quoted category word. Trajectory [4]: clue "This, an orzel in Poland, is seen on some of our coins" -> "White Eagle", where the gold is the bare common noun "eagle" (F1=2/3), i.e. the agent kept the descriptive lead adjective. Workflow step 3 ("reduce to the shortest canonical form: bare name, exact title, standard term") and the existing two-word-echo bullet already cover both forms, yet neither was followed. Note: the gate's per-case metrics disagree with these trajectory judgments (1f479608 and 3bffa7bff each score EM=1.0 in the gate baseline), so the surface form for the same entity is unstable across rollouts.
filler-adjective-clue-echo.label: filler-adjective-clue-echo

image-dependent-clue-unanswerable.description: Agent answered an image-dependent "seen here" clue with a plausible snack that does not match the gold, with no image available to disambiguate.
image-dependent-clue-unanswerable.evidence: Trajectory [13]: "Hostess snack food seen here split in half" → "Twinkie" (EM=0, F1=0); the clue depends on an image not present in the context.
image-dependent-clue-unanswerable.label: image-dependent-clue-unanswerable
image-dependent-clue-unanswerable.resolve_evidence: Trajectory [2]: an image-dependent "seen here" clue ("Seen here is the sock puppet version of this film, hidden on the DVD") was resolved correctly to "The Incredibles" with no image available (EM=1.0, F1=1.0). The triggering scenario is present and handled correctly, so the agent no longer defaults to an unverifiable plausible guess.

member-kind-clue-answered-with-org-name.description: Agent answers a "the alliance of these [member type]" clue with the organization's proper name instead of the member type the slot names.
member-kind-clue-answered-with-org-name.evidence: Trajectory [14]: "the alliance of these Chinese businesses" → predicted "Chinese Hand Laundry Alliance" (EM=0, F1=0.000); the slot asks for the member kind (e.g. laundries), not the org name.
member-kind-clue-answered-with-org-name.label: member-kind-clue-answered-with-org-name
member-kind-clue-answered-with-org-name.resolve_evidence: Trajectory [12]: member-kind clue 'A "letter to" this person, like Ben Bradlee...' was answered with the role/type 'editor' (the member kind), not a proper name or organization — correct, EM=1. Same scenario (clue asks for the kind given an example) handled correctly.

name-plus-event-clue-wrong-referent.description: Agent answers a bare 'name + event' clue with a specific participating person rather than the thing the event points to, yielding zero token overlap with the gold.
name-plus-event-clue-wrong-referent.evidence: Trajectory [14]: 'Henry Ward Beecherfor adultery' answered 'Theodore Tilton' (EM 0, F1 0.000); the named participant is a plausible co-referent of the event but shares no token with the gold.
name-plus-event-clue-wrong-referent.label: name-plus-event-clue-wrong-referent

nickname-vs-formal-given-name.description: Agent gave the diminutive "Patty" where the gold keeps the formal given name "Patricia"; the person was identified but the surface form lost EM.
nickname-vs-formal-given-name.evidence: Trajectory [3]: "Patty Hearst" vs gold "Patricia Hearst" (EM=0, F1=0.5). Contrast Trajectory [12] "Bob Mackie" scored correct with a nickname, so forcing formal given names is inconsistent with this batch — likely irreducible surface-form noise, not a safe rule fix.
nickname-vs-formal-given-name.label: nickname-vs-formal-given-name

official-institution-name-overused.description: Agent answers an institutional clue with the full official name when the gold uses the shorter common/brand form.
official-institution-name-overused.evidence: Trajectory [7]: clue 'this state university at Superior, not Madison'; agent answered 'University of Wisconsin–Superior' while the gold is the short form 'Wisconsin-Superior' (F1=0.667 token math: 2-of-2 gold tokens overlapped against 4 predicted tokens, so gold is the 2-word form); EM=0.
official-institution-name-overused.label: official-institution-name-overused
official-institution-name-overused.resolve_evidence: Trajectory [10]: the institutional clue "This spice company that owns Schilling is the largest producer of dehydrated garlic & onions" was answered with the short brand form "McCormick" and scored EM=1.0; the gate confirms the short form is what matches (the baseline rollout that used the fuller "McCormick & Company" form scored EM=0, F1=0.667). The scenario is triggered and handled correctly.

attempts.approach: Revised the People answer-form bullet to target the reference-work entry-name form and keep a conventionally attached title/byname (Sir, Saint, [name] the Great) while forbidding invented titles.

person-honorific-byname-omitted.description: Agent gives a person's bare name when the gold keeps a conventionally attached honorific ('Sir').
person-honorific-byname-omitted.evidence: Trajectory [12]: "In 1703 he became president of the Royal Society & was reelected annually until his death in 1727" answered "Isaac Newton" against a three-token gold "Sir Isaac Newton" (EM=0, F1=0.8), omitting the conventionally attached 'Sir' that the People answer-form rule explicitly requires.
person-honorific-byname-omitted.examples_state_evidence: The corresponding skill entry is the Answer Form "People" bullet, which contains only placeholder schemas ("the form a reference work would use as the entry name, e.g. `[first name] [last name]`; keep a title or byname that is conventionally attached (`Sir [name]`, `Saint [name]`, `[name] the Great`)"). No filled-in (correct, incorrect) pair such as "Sir Winston Churchill" not "Winston Churchill" is attached anywhere under it.
person-honorific-byname-omitted.label: person-honorific-byname-omitted

publication-name-type-word-omitted.description: Agent gave the bare masthead name for a publication-naming clue where the gold surface form carries an explicit publication-type word, so EM is lost even though the entity is right.
publication-name-type-word-omitted.evidence: Trajectory [5]: "In 1917 Scottish immigrant Bertie Charles Forbes began publishing a journal & gave it this name" -> predicted "Forbes" (EM=0, F1=0.667) against a two-token gold that adds the publication-type word; the clue gives no observable cue that the type word is required, and the bare name is the standard title of the magazine.
publication-name-type-word-omitted.label: publication-name-type-word-omitted

attempts.approach: Added a Common Failure Shapes bullet for the "A [category]: '[title]'" format: check whether a word in the quoted title is itself the name/term fitting the category before defaulting to the people associated with the work.

quoted-title-hides-answer-wordplay.description: Agent resolves a "A [category]: '[title]'" clue to the star of the titled work instead of finding the answer's name embedded as a word in the quoted title.
quoted-title-hides-answer-wordplay.evidence: Trajectory [1] ("A comedienne:\"Ball of Fire\""): agent answered "Barbara Stanwyck" (the 1941 film's lead), giving EM=0 and F1=0.000 — zero token overlap with the gold, meaning the gold is the name whose word is hidden in the title itself, not the film's cast member.
quoted-title-hides-answer-wordplay.examples_state_evidence: The corresponding skill entry is the Common Failure Shapes bullet for "A [category]: '[title]'" clues ("may hide the answer in the title itself — check whether a word in the title is a name or term that fits the category, and do not default to the people associated with the work"). It is stated entirely with the placeholders [category] and [title]; no concrete quoted title with its embedded answer word is given as an example pair.
quoted-title-hides-answer-wordplay.label: quoted-title-hides-answer-wordplay

singular-vs-plural-number-mismatch.description: Agent pluralizes a slotted answer that the clue frames as a single instance ("you're one of these"), losing EM to a singular gold form.
singular-vs-plural-number-mismatch.evidence: Trajectory [11]: clue "rise 5 ranks from Tenderfoot & you're one of these" answered "Eagle Scouts" (plural) vs singular gold "Eagle Scout" (EM=0, F1=0.500; the only differing token is number).
singular-vs-plural-number-mismatch.label: singular-vs-plural-number-mismatch

attempts.approach: Added a single-name clause to the People answer-form bullet so figures habitually referred to by one name (mononyms, many Roman figures) take that single name rather than the full formal lineage, while keeping the accepted honorific/byname clause intact.
Added a Common Failure Shapes bullet telling the agent to reuse the exact form the clue already supplies rather than expanding it with middle initials or extra qualifiers.

surplus-formal-name-parts.description: Agent produces a fuller person name than the gold, adding a middle initial that the gold omits.
surplus-formal-name-parts.evidence: Trajectory [9]: "On May 22, 1964 this president told America, 'The great society rests on abundance and liberty for all'" answered "Lyndon B. Johnson" against a two-token gold "Lyndon Johnson" (EM=0, F1=0.8 from the surplus middle initial).
surplus-formal-name-parts.label: surplus-formal-name-parts

surplus-title-translation-appended.description: Agent appended the English translation to a foreign-language film title, yielding a title longer than the gold.
surplus-title-translation-appended.evidence: Trajectory [5]: "Poet Pablo Neruda befriends the title character..." → "Il Postino: The Postman" (EM=0, F1=0.8); the gold is the shorter original title, so the trailing "The Postman" is surplus.
surplus-title-translation-appended.label: surplus-title-translation-appended

terse-format-clue-not-decoded.description: Agent answers a terse puzzle-format clue with the salient entity the clue's words evoke rather than decoding the format (expand an abbreviation; fill an ellipsis).
terse-format-clue-not-decoded.evidence: Trajectory [10]: clue "Let freedom ring: PHL" answered "Liberty Bell" (the object the phrase evokes) instead of the abbreviation's expansion (Philadelphia), EM=0/F1=0.000. Trajectory [15]: clue '"...on my mind"' answered "On My Mind", repeating the visible words instead of filling the ellipsis, EM=0/F1=0.000.
terse-format-clue-not-decoded.label: terse-format-clue-not-decoded

these-items-exhaustive-list.description: Agent answers a "these [items]" clue with an exhaustive enumeration of everything that qualifies instead of the small canonical member set.
these-items-exhaustive-list.evidence: Trajectory [3]: "Catgut comes from these animals" → predicted "Sheep, goats, cattle, hogs, horses, mules, and donkeys" (EM=0, F1=0.222); a canonical member or two was expected, not a full list.
these-items-exhaustive-list.label: these-items-exhaustive-list
these-items-exhaustive-list.resolve_evidence: Trajectory 6: 'These "soft-shell" animals are sometimes prepared & eaten without removing their eyes' → 'Crabs' — the canonical member set only, with no exhaustive enumeration of qualifying items; EM=1.0 / F1=1.0.

attempts.approach: Added a Common Failure Shapes bullet stating that 'current'/'today'/'now'/'recent' refer to when the clue was written; use the clue's other details (schools, dates, offices, achievements) to fix the era and the specific holder, and do not default to whoever holds the position today.

time-relative-clue-anchored-to-present.description: Agent reads "current"/"today"/"now" as the present day and answers with today's holder of a position, ignoring the clue's corroborating details that date it to an earlier era.
time-relative-clue-anchored-to-present.evidence: Trajectory [2]: "This current king of Jordan received part of his education in England at Harrow & Sandhurst" answered "Abdullah II" (zero token overlap); the Harrow+Sandhurst details point to King Hussein, who was 'current' when the clue was written, but the agent defaulted to the present king.
time-relative-clue-anchored-to-present.label: time-relative-clue-anchored-to-present

wrong-common-noun-term-selected.description: Agent answers a common-noun definitional clue with the base dictionary word, but the gold uses a different surface form of the same idea, producing zero token overlap.
wrong-common-noun-term-selected.evidence: Trajectory [12]: 'To cook food in liquid just below the boiling point' answered 'coddle' (EM 0, F1 0.000) — the identified technique matches the clue, but the gold's surface form shares no token with it.
wrong-common-noun-term-selected.label: wrong-common-noun-term-selected
wrong-common-noun-term-selected.resolve_evidence: Trajectory [3]: the common-noun definitional clue "The mouth of the Mississippi or a Helen Reddy 'Dawn'" was answered with exactly "Delta" (EM=1.0, F1=1.0) — the same surface form the gold uses, no paraphrase or zero-overlap synonym.

wrong-fruit-entity-knowledge-gap.description: Agent picks a fruit name that shares no token with the gold for a festival clue; a knowledge error not addressable by a skill rule.
wrong-fruit-entity-knowledge-gap.evidence: Trajectory [3]: predicted 'strawberry' for 'Oxnard festival for this fruit'; gold shares no token (EM=0, F1=0.000).
wrong-fruit-entity-knowledge-gap.label: wrong-fruit-entity-knowledge-gap

wrong-referent-film-riddle.evidence: Trajectory [15]: predicted 'Arnold Schwarzenegger' for \"In '84 he's a destroyer, in '82 he was just a barbarian\"; gold shares no token (EM=0, F1=0.000).
wrong-referent-film-riddle.label: wrong-referent-film-riddle
